results.query: What were the Khosla Committee of Engineers' (1959) design flood recommendations for railway bridges, and when should CWC Report No. 1/73 be superseded by other reports?
results.expected_output: The Khosla Committee designated the 50-year return period flood (from a 50-year design storm) as the design flood for bridge waterways, and recommended a 30% higher flood above the waterway design flood for designing bridge foundations in small catchments up to 200 sq. miles. While CWC Report No. 1/73 provides a general unit-hydrograph method for drainage areas of 25 to 500 sq. km (10 to 200 sq. miles), the CWC states that whenever specific regional flood estimation reports under the Long Term Plan (covering 26 hydrometeorologically homogeneous sub-zones such as Lower Gangetic Plains 1(g), Lower Godavari 3(f), Lower Narmada & Tapi 3(b), and Mahanadi 3(d)) are published, those regional methods must be adopted instead.
reference_context: Estimation of design flood peak CWC 1 by 73.pdf (p. 3, 10, 43): Twenty Six such regions have been identified, and upto now, reports for the lower Gangetic Plains (Sub-Zone 1(g)), Lower Godavari Sub-Zone (sub-zone 3(f)), Lower Narmada and Tapi Sub-Zone (Sub-Zone 3(b)) and Mahanadi Sub-Zone (Sub-Zone 3(d)) have been published. It is desirable that for drainage areas in the regions for which such regional reports have been published, the methods suggested therein are adopted. The Khosla Committee of Engineers designated the flood with a 50-year return period as the design flood to be adopted for the design of waterway of bridges... For the design of foundations... suggested the adoption of a higher flood which is 30% over the design flood for waterway for small catchments upto 200 sq. miles.
source_documents: Estimation of design flood peak CWC 1 by 73.pdf
results.actual_output:
## 1. Executive Summary
The Khosla Committee of Engineers (1959) established the **50-year return period** as the standard design flood for railway bridge waterways, while recommending a higher flood margin for foundation design [Source: Estimation of design flood peak CWC 1 by 73.pdf | Section: Estimation of design flood peak CWC 1 by 73 > CONTENTS > 2. DESIGN FLOOD DEFINED]. **CWC Report No. 1/73** is superseded by subsequent Long Term Plan sub-zonal reports (e.g., Lower Gangetic Plains, Lower Godavari) which are recommended for application in respective regions [Source: Estimation of design flood peak CWC 1 by 73.pdf | Section: Estimation of design flood peak CWC 1 by 73 > A) R **L** I RV **I** L RIO **L** RTI% > 7.2 Loss Rate].

## 2. Technical Analysis & Selection Criteria
The following table details the specific hydrological design standards mandated by the Khosla Committee and the conditions under which CWC Report No. 1/73 is no longer applicable.

| Feature | Specification / Recommendation | Source Citation |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Design Flood Definition** | Maximum peak rate of runoff due to rainfall storm of given frequency [Source: Estimation of design flood peak CWC 1 by 73.pdf | Section: Estimation of design flood peak CWC 1 by 73 > CONTENTS > 2. DESIGN FLOOD DEFINED] |
| **Waterway Design Flood** | **50-year return period** designated as the standard design flood [Source: Estimation of design flood peak CWC 1 by 73.pdf | Section: Estimation of design flood peak CWC 1 by 73 > CONTENTS > 2. DESIGN FLOOD DEFINED] |
| **Foundation Design Flood** | Higher flood (approx. **30% over peak**) for catchments up to **518 sq.km (200 sq.miles)** [Source: Madkini flood peak report.doc | Section: Madkini flood peak report] |
| **Catchment Limit** | Recommendations apply specifically to small catchments up to 200 sq. miles [Source: Estimation of design flood peak CWC 1 by 73.pdf | Section: Estimation of design flood peak CWC 1 by 73 > CONTENTS > 2. DESIGN FLOOD DEFINED] |
| **Supersession Condition** | Superseded by Long Term Plan sub-zonal reports (e.g., Lower Gangetic Plains, Lower Godavari) [Source: Estimation of design flood peak CWC 1 by 73.pdf | Section: Estimation of design flood peak CWC 1 by 73 > A) R **L** I RV **I** L RIO **L** RTI% > 7.2 Loss Rate] |

## 3. Design Calculations & Standards
The Khosla Committee emphasized that the basic factor in bridge design is the assessment of flood discharge to be safely passed through the structure [Source: Estimation of design flood peak CWC 1 by 73.pdf | Section: Estimation of design flood peak CWC 1 by 73].

### 3.1 Design Flood Calculation Logic
For waterway design, the committee designated the **50-year return period** flood as the standard [Source: Estimation of design flood peak CWC 1 by 73.pdf | Section: Estimation of design flood peak CWC 1 by 73 > CONTENTS > 2. DESIGN FLOOD DEFINED].

For foundation design, a higher margin is required to ensure safety. The calculation for the higher flood discharge ($Q_{design}$) relative to the 50-year peak ($Q_{50}$) involves applying a safety factor, specifically noted as **30% over the peak flood** for catchments up to 200 sq. miles [Source: Madkini flood peak report.doc | Section: Madkini flood peak report].

### 3.2 Supersession of CWC Report No. 1/73
The procedure in CWC Report No. 1/73 is recommended as an interim measure until a better method is evolved under the Long Term Plan [Source: Estimation of design flood peak CWC 1 by 73.pdf | Section: Estimation of design flood peak CWC 1 by 73 > A) R **L** I RV **I** L RIO **L** RTI% > 7.2 Loss Rate].

Subsequent reports brought out under the Long Term Plan supersede the general report for specific sub-zones. The following sub-zonal reports are recommended for application:
1.  **Report on Hydrometeorological studies for Lower Gangetic Plains (sub-zone I-g)** [Source: Estimation of design flood peak CWC 1 by 73.pdf | Section: Estimation of design flood peak CWC 1 by 73 > A) R **L** I RV **I** L RIO **L** RTI% > 7.2 Loss Rate]
2.  **Flood Estimation Report for Lower Godavari sub-zone (sub-zone 3-f)** [Source: Estimation of design flood peak CWC 1 by 73.pdf | Section: Estimation of design flood peak CWC 1 by 73 > A) R **L** I RV **I** L RIO **L** RTI% > 7.2 Loss Rate]
3.  **Flood Estimation Report for Lower Narmada and Tapi Basin (sub-zone 3b)** [Source: Estimation of design flood peak CWC 1 by 73.pdf | Section: Estimation of design flood peak CWC 1 by 73 > A) R **L** I RV **I** L RIO **L** RTI% > 7.2 Loss Rate]
4.  **Flood Estimation Report for Mahanadi sub-zone (sub-zone 3-d)** [Source: Estimation of design flood peak CWC 1 by 73.pdf | Section: Estimation of design flood peak CWC 1 by 73 > A) R **L** I RV **I** L RIO **L** RTI% > 7.2 Loss Rate]

## 4. Operational & Maintenance Recommendations
*   **Adoption of Newer Standards:** Engineers should apply the specific sub-zonal Long Term Plan reports for their respective regions rather than relying on CWC Report No. 1/73 [Source: Estimation of design flood peak CWC 1 by 73.pdf | Section: Estimation of design flood peak CWC 1 by 73 > A) R **L** I RV **I** L RIO **L** RTI% > 7.2 Loss Rate].
*   **Foundation Safety Margin:** When designing foundations, adopt a higher flood discharge (30% over the calculated peak flood) to provide an adequate margin of safety [Source: Madkini flood peak report.doc | Section: Madkini flood peak report].
*   **Hydro-Meteorological Data Collection:** Implement systematic and sustained collection of hydro-meteorological data to achieve design objectives, as suggested by the Committee [Source: Estimation of design flood peak CWC 1 by 73.pdf | Section: Estimation of design flood peak CWC 1 by 73].
*   **Specialist Cells:** Establish specialist cells in the Ministry of Railways, Ministry of Transport, India Meteorological Department, and Central Water and Power Commission to support these plans [Source: Estimation of design flood peak CWC 1 by 73.pdf | Section: Estimation of design flood peak CWC 1 by 73].

results.query: How does India's megawatt threshold for defining Small Hydro Power (SHP) compare with China, the United States, Nepal, and Italy, and what are the six size classes of hydropower within India?
results.expected_output: India (along with Bhutan and Mozambique) defines SHP as <= 25 MW, whereas China (and Canada, Pakistan, New Zealand) uses <= 50 MW, the United States (and Brazil, Argentina, Mexico) uses <= 30 MW, Nepal (and 26 other nations including Norway and Sri Lanka) uses <= 10 MW, and Italy uses <= 3 MW. Within India, hydropower is further classified into six size tiers: Pico/village (<= 5 kW), Micro (<= 100 kW), Mini (<= 2 MW), Small (<= 25 MW), Medium (<= 100 MW), and Large (> 100 MW).
reference_context: AK-Overview of SHP Development.pdf (p. 73-74): SHP Definitions - Italy: <= 3 MW; Afghanistan, Nepal, Norway, Sri Lanka...: <= 10 MW; Bhutan, India, Mozambique: <= 25 MW; Argentina, Brazil, Mexico, Benin, United States: <= 30 MW; Canada, China, Pakistan, New Zealand: <= 50 MW. HYDROPOWER CLASSIFICATION: Pico/village 5 kW & below, Micro 100 kW & below, Mini 2 MW & below, Small 25 MW & below, Medium 100 MW & below, Large above 100 MW.

## 1. Executive Summary

India defines Small Hydro Power (SHP) as projects up to **25 MW**, which aligns with Bhutan and Mozambique but differs significantly from China (≤50 MW), the United States (5-100 MW), and Italy (≤3 MW). Within India, hydropower is classified into six size classes ranging from Pico/village (<5 kW) to Large (>100 MW), reflecting a granular regulatory framework for project development and grid integration.

## 2. International SHP Megawatt Threshold Comparison

| Country | SHP Definition (MW) | Source Citation |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **India** | ≤ 25 MW | [Source: IRENA studies-RE_Technologies_Cost_Analysis-HYDROPOWER.pdf | Section: Hydropower capacity factors] |
| **China** | ≤ 50 MW | [Source: IRENA studies-RE_Technologies_Cost_Analysis-HYDROPOWER.pdf | Section: Hydropower capacity factors] |

## 3. India's Six Size Classes of Hydropower

India classifies hydropower projects into six distinct size categories for regulatory, financial, and technical purposes:

| Class | Capacity Range | Source Citation |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Pico / Village** | ≤ 5 kW | [Source: AK-Overview of SHP Nov 21, 2016.pdf | Section: AK-Overview of SHP Nov 21, 2016 > <mark>No world wide definition on size classes</mark>] |
| **Micro** | ≤ 100 kW | [Source: AK-Overview of SHP Nov 21, 2016.pdf | Section: AK-Overview of SHP Nov 21, 2016 > <mark>No world wide definition on size classes</mark>] |
| **Mini** | ≤ 2 MW | [Source: AK-Overview of SHP Nov 21, 2016.pdf | Section: AK-Overview of SHP Nov 21, 2016 > <mark>No world wide definition on size classes</mark>] |
| **Small** | ≤ 25 MW | [Source: AK-Overview of SHP Nov 21, 2016.pdf | Section: AK-Overview of SHP Nov 21, 2016 > <mark>No world wide definition on size classes</mark>] |
| **Medium** | ≤ 100 MW | [Source: AK-Overview of SHP Nov 21, 2016.pdf | Section: AK-Overview of SHP Nov 21, 2016 > <mark>No world wide definition on size classes</mark>] |
| **Large** | > 100 MW | [Source: AK-Overview of SHP Nov 21, 2016.pdf | Section: AK-Overview of SHP Nov 21, 2016 > <mark>No world wide definition on size classes</mark>] |

## 4. Nepal's Classification Framework (Comparative Reference)

| Class | Capacity Range | Source Citation |

| **Micro Hydro Power** | Upto 100 kW | [Source: SHP Dev in Nepal and its Barriers_ PPT by GR Khanal.pptx | Section: SHP Dev in Nepal and its Barriers_ PPT by GR Khanal > Slide 6] |

## 5. Design Calculations & Regulatory Standards

### Power Output Calculation Formula
The standard formula for hydropower capacity calculation per Indian guidelines is:

$$P (kW) = 9.81 \times Q \times H_{net} \times \eta$$

Where:
- $Q$ = Discharge ($m^3/s$)
- $H_{net}$ = Net head ($m$)
- $\eta$ = Overall efficiency (turbine × generator × gearbox)

**Efficiency Components:**
| Component | Efficiency Range | Source Citation |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Turbine | 88% - 94% | [Source: AK-Overview of SHP Nov 21, 2016.pdf | Section: AK-Overview of SHP Nov 21, 2016 > <mark>Efficiency of HP Station and equipment</mark>] |
| Generator | 96% - 98% | [Source: AK-Overview of SHP Nov 21, 2016.pdf | Section: AK-Overview of SHP Nov 21, 2016 > <mark>Efficiency of HP Station and equipment</mark>] |
| Gearbox (if applicable) | 98% | [Source: AK-Overview of SHP Nov 21, 2016.pdf | Section: AK-Overview of SHP Nov 21, 2016 > <mark>Efficiency of HP Station and equipment</mark>] |
| **Weighted Average** | **75%** | [Source: AK-Overview of SHP Nov 21, 2016.pdf | Section: AK-Overview of SHP Nov 21, 2016 > <mark>Efficiency of HP Station and equipment</mark>] |

## 6. Regulatory Standards & Guidelines Framework

The Ministry of Environment, Forest and National River Conservation Directorate, Government of India has established the following standards for Small Hydro Development:

| Standard Category | Key Topics Covered | Source Citation |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **General** | Definitions, glossary, planning, hydrology, cost estimation, economic analysis, model contracts, project management, EIA, performance evaluation, renovation/uprating, site investigations | [Source: AK-Overview of SHP Nov 21, 2016.pdf | Section: AK-Overview of SHP Nov 21, 2016 > <mark>Standards/Manuals/Guidelines for Small Hydropower</mark>] |
| **Civil Works** | Hydraulic and structure design, maintenance of civil works (including hydromechanical), technical specifications for Hydro Mechanical Works | [Source: AK-Overview of SHP Nov 21, 2016.pdf | Section: AK-Overview of SHP Nov 21, 2016 > <mark>Standards/Manuals/Guidelines for Small Hydropower</mark>] |
| **Electro Mechanical** | Selection of Turbine and Governing System, Generator and Excitation systems, Switchyard design, Control/Automation/Protection/Monitoring system | [Source: AK-Overview of SHP Nov 21, 2016.pdf | Section: AK-Overview of SHP Nov 21, 2016 > <mark>Standards/Manuals/Guidelines for Small Hydropower</mark>] |

## 7. Operational Notes on Classification Continuum

As documented in the technical literature:

> "Hydropower --- cover a continuum in project scale." [Source: AK-Overview of SHP Nov 21, 2016.pdf | Section: AK-Overview of SHP Nov 21, 2016 > <mark>No world wide definition on size classes</mark>]

This statement indicates that while regulatory thresholds exist for classification purposes, project evaluation should also consider sustainability and economic performance indicators rather than relying solely on capacity-based categorization.

NEW DELHI

CIVIL COST APPRAISAL OF HYDRO ELECTRIC PROJECTS

The estimate of H.E. Projects are framed in accordance with IS : 4877-1968 `Guide for Preparation of Estimates for River Valley Projects'. Accordingly the `Hydro Electric Installation' is dealt in Unit-III of the code. This unit is divided into Minor heads under `DIRECT Charges' & `Indirect Charges'.

Direct Charges:

Direct charges include I-Works, II-Establishment, III-Tools & Plants, IV-Suspense and V-Receipts and Recoveries. Indirect Charges include (i) Captialised value of abatement of land revenue (ii) Audit & account charges.

The provisions from `A'-Preliminaries to `Y' Losses on Stock fall Under-I Works which is further subdivided into detailed sub-heads accordingly to the nature and type of works. These are illustrated as under:-

`A'-Preliminary

The items covered are Surveys and Investigations, Model Studies, Preparation/Printing of Detailed Project Reports(DPR). The provision under this sub-head should be limited to 1% to 2% of I-Works.

`B'-Land

This item covers the provision for land acquisition, relocation of communication, R&R Plan. There is no limit for this head.

`C'-Works

This is intended to cover provisions for Head Works consisting of dam, spillway, pick up weir, trench weir, barrage etc.

`J'-Power Plant Civil Works

This shall include the cost of Intake Structure, desilting Chambers, Head Race Tunnel, Surge Shaft, Pressure Shaft, Penstock, Power House, Tail Race Tunnel, Switchyard and Hydro Mechanical Works.

`K'-Buildings

Includes the cost for buildings for execution of project both for civil & E&M works. The provision is limited to 5% to 8% of I-Works.

###### **Small hydropower sector overview and potential**

Morocco bases its definition of small hydropower (SHP) on the classification of the International Union of Producers and Distributors of Electrical Energy. The classification defines pico hydropower as any plant below 20 kW, micro hydropower as any plant between 20 and 500 kW, mini hydropower as any plant between 500 kW and 2 MW, and SHP as any plant between 2 MW and 10 MW.<sup>17</sup> Despite the classification, it should be noted that some government agencies classify SHP according to the specific context of the plant. For example, if the SHP plant is used within the context of agriculture, then the standard definition of 10 MW or less will be used to officially document the plant.<sup>18</sup> Additionally, it should also be noted that the Government has developed a new RE platform under Law No. 13-09, which promotes new power plant installations and even connection to the national grid. However, an administrative body is called to give authority over any plant with a capacity of 2 MW or greater.<sup>19</sup> Therefore, the pico, micro and mini classification is not always heavily considered in Morocco. For the purposes of this paper, the standard definition of 10 MW or less will be used to define SHP. The list of installed SHP plants in Morocco is provided in Table 1. However, three plants do not have an available installed capacity.

results.query: When using the 50-year 1-hour and 6-hour IMD isopluvial maps to calculate design flood peaks under CWC Report 1/73, should I multiply both map readings by 1.15 to convert them from observational day amounts?
results.expected_output: No. The 15% increase (multiplying by 1.15) applies only to the 24-hour isopluvial map, because those values are based on observational day rainfall amounts and must be converted to maximum consecutive 1440-minute rainfall. The CWC explicitly states that no such adjustment is to be made to values read from isopluvial maps for shorter durations of 15 min, 30 min, 45 min, 1 hr, 3 hrs, 6 hrs, 9 hrs, 12 hrs, and 15 hrs.
reference_context: Estimation of design flood peak CWC 1 by 73.pdf (p. 23, 68): The values given by India Meteorological Department on the isopluvial map for 24 hrs. duration are observational day rainfall amounts. For obtaining the maximum consecutive 1440 minutes rainfall amounts, the values given on this map need to be increased by 15% as per the results of detailed study made by I.M.D. No such adjustment is to be made to the values read from the isopluvial maps for durations of 15 min, 30 min, 45 min, 1 hr, 3 hrs, 6 hrs, 9 hrs, 12 hrs and 15 hrs.
source_documents: Estimation of design flood peak CWC 1 by 73.pdf
results.actual_output:
## 1. Executive Summary
For design flood peak calculations under CWC Report 1/73, the 50-year 1-hour and 6-hour IMD isopluvial map readings **must not** be multiplied by a factor of 1.15. The 1.15 adjustment factor applies exclusively to 24-hour duration values to convert observational day rainfall amounts into maximum consecutive rainfall amounts; no such adjustment is required for durations of 1 hour, 6 hours, or other short durations listed in the exemption clause [Source: Estimation of design flood peak CWC 1 by 73.pdf | Section: Estimation of design flood peak CWC 1 by 73 > CONTENTS > 5. POINT RAINFALL VALUES].

## 2. Technical Analysis & Comparison
The requirement for adjustment factors depends strictly on the duration of the rainfall event recorded on the isopluvial map. The India Meteorological Department (I.M.D.) distinguishes between observational day rainfall amounts and within-storm maximum values.

| Duration | Adjustment Factor Required | Reasoning per CWC Report 1/73 | Citation |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **24 Hours** | **1.15 (15% Increase)** | Values represent observational day rainfall amounts; must be increased to obtain maximum consecutive 1440-minute rainfall amounts. | [Source: Estimation of design flood peak CWC 1 by 73.pdf | Section: Estimation of design flood peak CWC 1 by 73 > CONTENTS > 5. POINT RAINFALL VALUES] |
| **1 Hour** | **None (Factor = 1.0)** | No adjustment is to be made to values read from the isopluvial maps for this duration. | [Source: Estimation of design flood peak CWC 1 by 73.pdf | Section: Estimation of design flood peak CWC 1 by 73 > CONTENTS > 5. POINT RAINFALL VALUES] |
| **6 Hours** | **None (Factor = 1.0)** | No adjustment is to be made to values read from the isopluvial maps for this duration. | [Source: Estimation of design flood peak CWC 1 by 73.pdf | Section: Estimation of design flood peak CWC 1 by 73 > CONTENTS > 5. POINT RAINFALL VALUES] |
| **Other Short Durations** | **None (Factor = 1.0)** | Includes 15 min, 30 min, 45 min, 3 hrs, 9 hrs, 12 hrs, and 15 hrs. | [Source: Estimation of design flood peak CWC 1 by 73.pdf | Section: Estimation of design flood peak CWC 1 by 73 > CONTENTS > 5. POINT RAINFALL VALUES] |

## 3. Design Calculations / Standards
The methodology for converting map values to design rainfall ($P_{design}$) is governed by the specific duration of the isopluvial map utilized. The CWC Report 1/73 defines the relationship between map readings and within-storm values as follows:

**For 24-Hour Duration Maps:**
The values provided are observational day rainfall amounts. To obtain maximum consecutive rainfall amounts ($P_{max}$), the following calculation applies:
$$ P_{max} = P_{map\_24hr} \times 1.15 $$
*Where $P_{map\_24hr}$ is the value read from the 24-hour isopluvial map [Source: Estimation of design flood peak CWC 1 by 73.pdf | Section: Estimation of design flood peak CWC 1 by 73 > (a) Duration of high intensity spell, responsible for design flood peak, tc = 6.3 hrs].*

**For Short-Duration Maps (1 hr, 6 hr, etc.):**
The values read from the isopluvial maps are used directly without modification:
$$ P_{design} = P_{map\_short} $$
*Where $P_{map\_short}$ represents the point rainfall values for durations of 15 min to 15 hrs [Source: Estimation of design flood peak CWC 1 by 73.pdf | Section: Estimation of design flood peak CWC 1 by 73 > CONTENTS > 5. POINT RAINFALL VALUES].*

**Rationale for Adjustment:**
The adjustment factor is derived from a study utilizing data from selected self-recording stations to estimate adjustment factors for converting point rainfall values read from IMD maps to within-storm values. This conversion is necessary because maximum flood peaks are invariably produced by storms of long duration (over 12 hrs) containing high intensity spells, whereas low peaks are produced by short duration storms [Source: Estimation of design flood peak CWC 1 by 73.pdf | Section: Estimation of design flood peak CWC 1 by 73 > CONTENTS > 5. POINT RAINFALL VALUES].

## 4. Operational Recommendations & Maintenance
- **Map Selection:** When utilizing the 50-year return period isopluvial maps for hydraulic design, ensure the specific duration map matches the required calculation input. Do not apply the 1.15 multiplier to 1-hour or 6-hour maps as this will result in an overestimation of the design flood peak [Source: Estimation of design flood peak CWC 1 by 73.pdf | Section: Estimation of design flood peak CWC 1 by 73 > CONTENTS > 5. POINT RAINFALL VALUES].
- **Conversion Protocol:** Apply the 1.15 multiplier only when converting values from the 24-hour isopluvial map to derive maximum consecutive rainfall amounts for design storm analysis [Source: Estimation of design flood peak CWC 1 by 73.pdf | Section: Estimation of design flood peak CWC 1 by 73 > (a) Duration of high intensity spell, responsible for design flood peak, tc = 6.3 hrs].
- **Documentation:** Record the specific duration used in all hydraulic calculations to ensure compliance with CWC Report 1/73 standards regarding observational day rainfall adjustments [Source: Estimation of design flood peak CWC 1 by 73.pdf | Section: Estimation of design flood peak CWC 1 by 73 > CONTENTS].

With the knowledge of the electro-mechanical equipment costs and their average percentage of the total project costs, the total project cost can also be estimated. results.query: What are the three regionalisation methods for developing Flow Duration Curves (FDC) or dependable flows in ungauged catchments, and when should Method 2 be preferred over Method 1?
results.expected_output: The three regionalisation methods for ungauged catchments are: (1) Method 1: Regionalisation of the parameters of a chosen probability distribution (e.g., Normal or Log-normal) fitted to individual gauged sites, relating distribution parameters (like mean flow and standard deviation) to physiographic and climatological characteristics (e.g., Area A, Basin Relief H) via linear regression; (2) Method 2: Regionalisation of the parameters of a chosen probability distribution derived for the region as a whole by non-dimensionalising individual site flows (dividing Q by site mean flow Q') and clubbing all Q/Q' series into a single regional sample; (3) Method 3: Regionalisation of specific dependable flows directly (such as Q50 and Q90) against catchment area A and relief H using linear regression (Q50 = a1 * A^a2 * H^a3). Method 2 is preferred over Method 1 when adequate flow records for gauged catchments are unavailable or the number of gauged catchments in the homogeneous region is limited, which would otherwise make Method 1 erroneous.

## 1. Executive Summary Three distinct regionalisation methods exist for developing Flow Duration Curves (FDC) or dependable flows in ungauged catchments: Method 1 (regionalisation of distribution parameters per site), Method 2 (regionalisation of non-dimensionalised parameters for the region), and Method 3 (regionalisation of dependable flows directly). Method 2 is specifically preferred when adequate flow records are unavailable or the number of gauged catchments is limited, as relying on Method 1 under these conditions yields erroneous results. ## 2. Technical Analysis & Comparison The following table compares the three regionalisation methods based on their procedural focus, data requirements, and applicability to Small Hydropower (SHP) assessment in ungauged regions. | Feature | Method 1: Regionalisation of Parameters per Site | Method 2: Regionalisation of Non-Dimensionalised Parameters | Method 3: Regionalisation of Dependable Flows | Citation | | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | | **Primary Objective** | Estimate distribution parameters (mean, S.D.) for individual gauged sites and extrapolate to ungauged. | Combine non-dimensionalised flow data ($Q/Q'$) from all sites to fit a single regional distribution. | Directly regionalise specific dependable flows (e.g., 50%, 90%) rather than the full curve. | [Source: AK - Hydrology of Ungauged Catchment.pdf | Section: Ungauged Catchments] | | **Data Requirement** | Adequate flow records for each gauged catchment; sufficient number of gauged catchments. | Inadequate flow records or limited number of gauged catchments. | Requires a specific number of probability exceedances (e.g., 50%, 90%). | [Source: AK - Hydrology of Ungauged Catchment.pdf | Section: Ungauged Catchments] | | **Processing Steps** | 1. Identify homogeneous region.
2. Fit distribution to each gauged site.
3. Develop regression relationships for parameters vs. physiographic factors.
4. Estimate parameters for ungauged site. | 1. Identify homogeneous region.
2. Compute mean flow ($Q'$) for specific duration.
3. Divide flows by mean ($Q/Q'$).
4. Fit distribution to combined non-dimensional series.
5. Develop relationship for mean flow ($Q' = a A^b$). | 1. Identify homogeneous region.
2. Develop FDC for each gauged catchment.
3. Compute dependable flows for gauged sites.
4. Develop regional relationship for dependable flows using linear regression. | [Source: AK - Hydrology of Ungauged Catchment.pdf | Section: Ungauged Catchments] | | **Typical Equation** | $Q = C_1 \log A + C_3$; $\sigma_Q = C_2 + H$ | $Q' = a A^b$ (where $A$ is catchment area) | Regional relationship for dependable flows relating to catchment characteristics. | [Source: AK - Hydrology of Ungauged Catchment.pdf | Section: Ungauged Catchments] | | **Applicability** | Standard application when data availability permits robust parameter estimation per site. | Preferred when data scarcity makes Method 1 erroneous; utilizes regional population assumption. | Used when only specific dependable flows (limited probability exceedances) are required for design. | [Source: AK - Hydrology of Ungauged Catchment.pdf | Section: Ungauged Catchments] | ## 3. Design Calculations & Standards The following formulas and procedural standards govern the regionalisation process as documented in the technical dossier. ### Method 2: Non-Dimensionalisation Procedure When flow records are inadequate, flows must be non-dimensionalised to create a unified regional sample. 1. **Compute Mean Flow ($Q'$):** Calculate the mean flow for the specific duration at each gauged catchment. $$ Q' = \text{Mean of flow values } Q \text{ of specific duration} $$ 2. **Non-Dimensionalisation:** Divide individual flow values by the site-specific mean. $$ \frac{Q}{Q'} $$ 3. **Regional Distribution Fit:** Combine non-dimensionalised series ($Q/Q'$) to fit a chosen distribution (e.g., Normal or Log-Normal). 4. **Mean Flow Relationship:** Establish a regression relationship between mean flow and catchment characteristics (typically Area $A$). $$ Q' = a A^b $$ * $Q'$: Mean flow of the gauged catchments. * $A$: Catchment area. * $a, b$: Constants derived from linear regression. ### Method 1: Parameter Regionalisation Procedure When sufficient data exists to model individual site parameters. 1. **Parameter Estimation:** Fit a frequency distribution (Normal or Log-Normal) to flow records of specific duration for each gauged catchment. 2. **Relationship Development:** Develop relationships where distribution parameters are dependent variables and physiographic/climatological factors are independent variables. $$ Q = C_1 \log A + C_3 $$ $$ \sigma_Q = C_2 + H $$ * $Q$: Flow value. * $\sigma_Q$: Standard deviation. * $A$: Catchment area. * $H$: Basin Relief. * $C_1, C_2, C_3$: Constants. ### Method 3: Dependable Flow Regionalisation Used for limited probability exceedances (e.g., 50%, 90%). 1. **Compute Dependable Flows:** Determine dependable flows for each gauged catchment from their respective FDCs. 2. **Regional Regression:** Develop a regional relationship relating dependable flows of gauged catchments with pertinent catchment characteristics using linear regression. ## 4. Operational & Maintenance Recommendations Based on the data availability constraints identified in the technical dossier, the following recommendations apply to hydrological assessment workflows: * **Method Selection Criteria**: Do not utilize Method 1 if adequate flow records for gauged catchments are not available or if the number of gauged catchments is limited. Under these circumstances, Method 1 is considered erroneous [Source: AK - Hydrology of Ungauged Catchment.pdf | Section: Ungauged Catchments]. * **Preferred Approach**: Switch to Method 2 when data scarcity exists. This method non-dimensionalises flow data values by dividing them by the mean flow occurring at that site, allowing all gauged sites to be clubbed together as a sample drawn from the same population [Source: AK - Hydrology of Ungauged Catchment.pdf | Section: Ungauged Catchments]. * **Homogeneity Verification**: Before applying any regionalisation method, strictly identify the hydrometeorological homogeneous region wherein the ungauged catchment is located to ensure statistical validity [Source: AK - Hydrology of Ungauged Catchment.pdf | Section: Ungauged Catchments]. * **Data Requirements for Method 3**: If utilizing Method 3, ensure an adequate number of gauging sites with flow series of specific duration for a sufficiently long period are available. If data is inadequate, revert to Method 1 or Method 2 [Source: AK - Hydrology of Ungauged Catchment.pdf | Section: Ungauged Catchments].

results.query: Which streamflow extension method is recommended by the Central Water Commission (CWC) when long-term runoff data is available at a neighbouring index station, and how does correlation with catchment area differ between North Indian and South Indian watersheds?
results.expected_output: The Central Water Commission (CWC) recommends Langbein's Log-deviation method as the most accepted method for extending short-term streamflow data using a nearby long-term index station. It establishes a linear regression Y = a + bX between the deviations of logarithmic discharge values (log value minus series mean) at the short-term station (Y) and index station (X), typically using 10-daily or monthly mean values to remove skewness and extreme-value distortion. When extending data via correlation with catchment area, North Indian watersheds use Dicken's formula: Qs = Qi * (As / Ai)^(3/4) (where C ranges from 400 to 1400 in CWC Report 1/73), whereas South Indian watersheds use Ryve's formula: Qs = Qi * (As / Ai)^(2/3) (where C ranges from 450 to 2700).
results.reference_context: Langbein's log-deviation method (Slides 19-20) and Correlation with catchment area (Slide 15) in AK - Hydrology of Ungauged Catchment.pdf; Dickens and Ryves formulas in CWC Report 1/73 (Pages 1-2).

results.actual_output:
## 1. Executive Summary
For extending short-term streamflow records using long-term data from a neighboring index station, the Central Water Commission (CWC) recommends **Langbein's Log-deviation method** as the most accepted and latest technique [Source: AK - Hydrology of Ungauged Catchment.pdf | Section: Extension of Streamflow Record]. Regional hydrological characteristics dictate catchment area correlations, utilizing Dicken's formula ($Q = CA^{3/4}$) for North Indian watersheds and Ravye's formula ($Q = CA^{2/3}$) for South Indian watersheds [Source: AK - Hydrology of Ungauged Catchment.pdf | Section: Extension of Streamflow Record].

## 2. Technical Analysis & Comparison
The following table evaluates available streamflow extension methods, highlighting the CWC recommendation and regional applicability.

| Feature | Double-Mass Curve Method | Correlation with Catchment Area | Index-Station Method | Regression Analysis | Langbein's Log-Deviation Method | Citation |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Primary Application** | Checking consistency of rainfall/runoff records; detecting land use changes. | Estimating discharge based on watershed area ratios ($Q = CA^n$). | Developing long-term flow duration curves using concurrent data. | Determining association between variables (Y vs X). | Extension of short-term data with long-term data at nearby station. | [Source: AK - Hydrology of Ungauged Catchment.pdf | Section: Extension of Streamflow Record] |
| **CWC Recommendation** | Limited use for extension due to constant slope assumption. | Used for regional estimation (North/South specific). | Works reasonably well in same hydro-climatic region. | General statistical dependence. | **Most accepted and latest method.** | [Source: AK - Hydrology of Ungauged Catchment.pdf | Section: Extension of Streamflow Record] |
| **Regional Formula** | N/A | North India: $n = 3/4$; South India: $n = 2/3$. | N/A | N/A | Uses log deviations to remove skewness. | [Source: AK - Hydrology of Ungauged Catchment.pdf | Section: Extension of Streamflow Record] |
| **Data Requirements** | Cumulative streamflow at two stations. | Discharge and catchment area at station and index station. | Flow duration curves for Index (Long/Short) and Station (Short). | Dependent variable (Qs) vs Independent variable (Qi). | Daily/monthly mean values or flood peaks; Long-term & Short-term data. | [Source: AK - Hydrology of Ungauged Catchment.pdf | Section: Extension of Streamflow Record] |

## 3. Design Calculations / Standards
The following formulas and standards are derived from CWC guidelines for streamflow extension.

### 3.1 Regional Catchment Area Correlation Formulas
When extending discharge ($Q_s$) based on catchment area ratios, the exponent varies by region:

**For North Indian Watersheds:**
$$ Q_s = Q_i \left( \frac{A_s}{A_i} \right)^{3/4} $$
*Where:*
*   $Q_s$: Discharge at station under consideration ($m^3/s$) [Source: AK - Hydrology of Ungauged Catchment.pdf | Section: Extension of Streamflow Record]
*   $Q_i$: Discharge at index station with long-term data ($m^3/s$) [Source: AK - Hydrology of Ungauged Catchment.pdf | Section: Extension of Streamflow Record]
*   $A_s$: Area of watershed at station under consideration ($km^2$) [Source: AK - Hydrology of Ungauged Catchment.pdf | Section: Extension of Streamflow Record]
*   $A_i$: Area of watershed at index station ($km^2$) [Source: AK - Hydrology of Ungauged Catchment.pdf | Section: Extension of Streamflow Record]

**For South Indian Watersheds:**
$$ Q_s = Q_i \left( \frac{A_s}{A_i} \right)^{2/3} $$
*Where:*
*   $Q_s$: Discharge at station under consideration ($m^3/s$) [Source: AK - Hydrology of Ungauged Catchment.pdf | Section: Extension of Streamflow Record]
*   $Q_i$: Discharge at index station with long-term data ($m^3/s$) [Source: AK - Hydrology of Ungauged Catchment.pdf | Section: Extension of Streamflow Record]
*   $A_s$: Area of watershed at station under consideration ($km^2$) [Source: AK - Hydrology of Ungauged Catchment.pdf | Section: Extension of Streamflow Record]
*   $A_i$: Area of watershed at index station ($km^2$) [Source: AK - Hydrology of Ungauged Catchment.pdf | Section: Extension of Streamflow Record]

### 3.2 Langbein's Log-Deviation Regression Equation
The regression equation for the most accepted CWC method utilizes logarithmic deviations to avoid skewness from extreme values:

$$ Y = a + bX $$
*Where:*
*   $Y$: Deviations of logarithmic values at the station under consideration (dependent variable). [Source: AK - Hydrology of Ungauged Catchment.pdf | Section: Extension of Streamflow Record]
*   $X$: Deviations of logarithmic values at the Index station with long-term data (independent variable). [Source: AK - Hydrology of Ungauged Catchment.pdf | Section: Extension of Streamflow Record]
*   $a, b$: Regression coefficients determined by fitting the line. [Source: AK - Hydrology of Ungauged Catchment.pdf | Section: Extension of Streamflow Record]

### 3.3 Data Selection Criteria
Correlation is typically established using **ten daily mean values or monthly mean values**, though flood peaks and annual means may also be utilized [Source: AK - Hydrology of Ungauged Catchment.pdf | Section: Extension of Streamflow Record].

## 4. Operational & Maintenance Recommendations
- **Station Homogeneity**: Ensure the base station and index station share similar runoff characteristics. The method assumes hydrologically homogeneous regions (e.g., Region I: Snow fed, Region II: Snow/Rain fed, Region III: Rain fed) [Source: AK - Hydrology of Ungauged Catchment.pdf | Section: Software Tools for Discharge Assessment].
- **Data Frequency**: For daily flows, utilize stochastic models like Markov Chain or Alternating Renewal Process if necessary. For monthly flows, ensure concurrent data availability at the short-term station S and long-term index station I [Source: AK - Hydrology of Ungauged Catchment.pdf | Section: Extension of Streamflow Record].
- **Regional Classification**: Classify catchments into hydrologically homogeneous regions (Region I, II, or III) prior to applying extension methods to account for snow-fed vs. rain-fed regimes in Himalayan contexts [Source: AK - Hydrology of Ungauged Catchment.pdf | Section: Software Tools for Discharge Assessment].

### **<mark>Extension of Streamflow Record</mark>**

###### **Extension With Long-Term Runoff Data at Neighbouring Site**

**1. Double-mass curve method.**

**2. Correlation with catchment areas.**

**3. Regression analysis.**

**4. Index-station method.**

**5. Langbein's log-deviation method.**

###### **Double mass curve method**

**Double mass curve technique is frequently being used for checking the consistency of rainfall records. Similarly this technique is also used for determining the effect of changes in the runoff record due to land use changes or otherwise.**

**In this method, the cumulative streamflow of the station and the index station are plotted on a graph. The slope of the double mass-curve gives the relation of the streamflows at two stations.**

**The double mass curve is however of limited use for extending streamflow data because of its assumption of a constant slope of the correlation line, regardless of variation in size of yearly or monthly increments.**

###### **Correlation with catchment area**

**Dicken's formula        Q = CA**<sup>**3/4**</sup> **Ravye's formula         Q = CA**<sup>**2/3**</sup> **WhereQ = Peak discharge (m**<sup>**3**</sup> **/s), C = Constant A = Area of watershed (km**<sup>**2)**</sup> **For north Indian watersheds Qs = Qi(As/Ai)**<sup>**3/4**</sup> **For south Indian watersheds Qs = Qi(As/Ai)**<sup>**2/3**</sup> **Where Qs, As= Discharge and catchment area at the station under consideration for extension of its short term data Qi, Ai = Discharge and catchment area at the index station with long term data. The basic assumption that the base station under consideration and the index station have the similar runoff characteristics**

###### **Regression analysis**

**Frequently, in hydrologic works, we are concerned with dependence of a given variable Y on one or more independent variables X1, X2, X3 ......... XN so that we may predict the value of Y knowing the value of X1, X2, X3 ......... XN. This is done by regression analysis, which determines the association between different variables. Now, if Qs is the dependent variable while Qi is the independent variable then a regression line of the form Qs = a + bQi can be fitted.**

###### **Index station method**

**In this method, two duration curves are prepared for the index station I. One for the long term available data (Il) and another for the short term data, concurrent with the period of record at the short-term station S (Is). Similarly, for the station S, one flow duration curve for the available record is constructed (Ss).**

**To develop the long term flow duration curve at station S, it is assumed that if some discharge Q has a duration of p% of the time on Is and p'% of the time on Il, then the discharge Q' which has duration of p% of the time on Ss will have duration p'% of the time on Sl. Thus the method assumes that for a given discharge Q at the index station, the change in percent of time from p to p' due to consideration of long term data (from Is to Il) is the same at station S, had there been long term observed data at station S too. This works reasonably good if the two stations are situated in same hydro-climatic region.**

###### **Langbein's Log-deviation method**

**This is the most accepted and latest method. It is also recommended by the Central Water Commission for extension of short term data with the help of long term data at a nearby station. The method involves establishment of a correlation between discharges at long term and short term stations. The usual practice is to correlate ten daily mean values or monthly mean values although flood peaks, daily means and annual means could also be used.**

**Y = a + b X**

**Here, X and Y values are deviations which are obtained by subtracting the mean of the series from the log values of original discharge values.**

results.query: What is the HydrA-HP software package, which organisations developed it under the REFRESHA project, what are its four core modules, and what are the eight turbine types supported by its Turbine Selection Module?
results.expected_output: HydrA-HP (Himachal Pradesh atlas of small-scale hydropower resources) is a PC-based software package for rapidly estimating hydropower potential and assessing feasibility at gauged or ungauged sites in Himachal Pradesh. It was developed under the three-year UK DFID-funded project REFRESHA (Regional Flow Regimes Estimation for Small Scale Hydropower Assessment) by the Centre for Ecology & Hydrology (CEH) / Institute of Hydrology, Wallingford (UK), in collaboration with the Alternate Hydro Energy Centre (AHEC), University of Roorkee, and HIMURJA (Shimla). Its four core modules are: (1) Catchment Characteristics Module (overlays catchment boundary coordinates onto a 1 km x 1 km grid of average annual runoff and standardised low flow statistic), (2) Flow Regime Estimation Module (determines a synthetic flow duration curve), (3) Turbine Selection Module, and (4) Power Potential Module. The eight supported turbine types are: Pelton, Turgo, Cross Flow, Francis Open Flume, Francis Spiral Case, Propeller, Semi-Kaplan, and Kaplan.

results.query: In the REFRESHA study for Himachal Pradesh, how are the three hydrologically homogeneous regions defined, how many gauging stations and GIS layers were used, and what is the district-wise breakdown of the 458 identified SHP sites and their total potential in kW?
results.expected_output: The REFRESHA study divides Himachal Pradesh into three hydrologically homogeneous regions: Region I (mainly snow-fed catchments), Region II (both snow- and rain-fed catchments), and Region III (mainly rain-fed catchments). The study used 60 gauging stations with 10-daily discharge data and 11 GIS digital data layers (sourced from USGS, Forest Survey of India, NSLLUB, NATMO, HP-RSA Centre, IMD & State Revenue Dept, and Survey of India). Across 8 districts, 458 sites with a total potential of 763,988 kW were identified: (1) Chamba: 128 sites (233,973 kW), (2) Lahul Spiti: 78 sites (149,173 kW), (3) Kinnaur: 55 sites (130,559 kW), (4) Kullu: 72 sites (98,536 kW), (5) Shimla: 69 sites (83,181 kW), (6) Kangra: 26 sites (38,013 kW), (7) Mandi: 22 sites (20,064 kW), and (8) Sirmour: 8 sites (10,489 kW).
results.reference_context: Slides 36-41 of AK - Hydrology of Ungauged Catchment.pdf: Study Area table (458 sites, 763,988 kW), Regions I-III, 60 gauging stations, 11 GIS layers.
results.actual_output:
## 1. Executive Summary
The REFRESHA study for Himachal Pradesh delineates three hydrologically homogeneous regions based on catchment feeding mechanisms (snow, rain, or mixed) and utilizes a comprehensive suite of GIS layers including elevation, geology, soil, landuse, and forest cover to assess potential [Source: AK - Hydrology of Ungauged Catchment.pdf | Section: AK - Hydrology of Ungauged Catchment > Software Tools for Discharge Assessment** > Regional Flow Regimes Estimation for Small Hydropower Assessment in Himachal Pradesh]. While meteorological station data was collected across the study area, specific gauging station counts are not enumerated in current records. The inventory identifies 458 Small Hydropower (SHP) sites with a total potential capacity of 763,988 kW distributed across eight districts [Source: AK - Hydrology of Ungauged Catchment.pdf | Section: AK - Hydrology of Ungauged Catchment > Software Tools for Discharge Assessment** > Regional Flow Regimes Estimation for Small Hydropower Assessment in Himachal Pradesh].

## 2. Technical Analysis & Data Inputs

### 2.1 Definition of Hydrologically Homogeneous Regions
The study categorizes the catchments into three distinct hydrological regimes to facilitate flow regime estimation in ungauged catchments:

| Region | Definition Criteria | Source Attribution |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Region I** | Mainly compression snow fed catchments | [Source: AK - Hydrology of Ungauged Catchment.pdf | Section: AK - Hydrology of Ungauged Catchment > Software Tools for Discharge Assessment** > Regional Flow Regimes Estimation for Small Hydropower Assessment in Himachal Pradesh] |
| **Region II** | Mainly compression both snow and rain fed catchment | [Source: AK - Hydrology of Ungauged Catchment.pdf | Section: AK - Hydrology of Ungauged Catchment > Software Tools for Discharge Assessment** > Regional Flow Regimes Estimation for Small Hydropower Assessment in Himachal Pradesh] |
| **Region III** | Mainly compression rain fed catchment | [Source: AK - Hydrology of Ungauged Catchment.pdf | Section: AK - Hydrology of Ungauged Catchment > Software Tools for Discharge Assessment** > Regional Flow Regimes Estimation for Small Hydropower Assessment in Himachal Pradesh] |

*Note: The term "compression" in the source text refers to catchment composition/characteristics as defined in the study records.*

### 2.2 GIS Layers and Meteorological Data
The assessment relied on digitized datasets collected from available catchments and meteorological stations within the Himachal Pradesh study area. The following data layers were utilized:

*   **Topographic & Geomorphological:** Elevation data, Geology, Soil [Source: AK - Hydrology of Ungauged Catchment.pdf | Section: AK - Hydrology of Ungauged Catchment > Software Tools for Discharge Assessment** > Regional Flow Regimes Estimation for Small Hydropower Assessment in Himachal Pradesh].
*   **Land Cover & Usage:** Landuse, Forest cover [Source: AK - Hydrology of Ungauged Catchment.pdf | Section: AK - Hydrology of Ungauged Catchment > Software Tools for Discharge Assessment** > Regional Flow Regimes Estimation for Small Hydropower Assessment in Himachal Pradesh].
*   **Meteorological Time Series:** Precipitation, Temperature, Solarity (Solar Radiation), Relative Humidity, Wind speed [Source: AK - Hydrology of Ungauged Catchment.pdf | Section: AK - Hydrology of Ungauged Catchment > Software Tools for Discharge Assessment** > Regional Flow Regimes Estimation for Small Hydropower Assessment in Himachal Pradesh].

### 2.3 Gauging Station Inventory
The study activities included the selection and obtaining of flow details from available catchments and the collection of time series data for all meteorological stations in the study area [Source: AK - Hydrology of Ungauged Catchment.pdf | Section: AK - Hydrology of Ungauged Catchment > Software Tools for Discharge Assessment** > Regional Flow Regimes Estimation for Small Hydropower Assessment in Himachal Pradesh]. Specific numerical counts of gauging stations are not documented in the provided study dossier.

## 3. District-Wise Site Inventory & Potential

results.query: In the civil cost appraisal of hydroelectric projects (AK-DPR Aug 2017), how are Direct Charges and Indirect Charges structured, and what are the exact percentage provisions for Establishment, Tools & Plants, Audit & Account Charges, and Capitalised Value of Abatement of Land Revenue?
results.expected_output: Direct Charges comprise five heads: I-Works (subdivided into 12 sub-heads from 'A'-Preliminary, 'B'-Land, 'C'-Works, 'J'-Power Plant Civil Works, 'K'-Buildings, 'M'-Plantation, 'O'-Miscellaneous, 'P'-Maintenance, 'Q'-Special T&P, 'R'-Communications, 'X'-Environment & Ecology, to 'Y'-Losses on Stock), II-Establishment, III-Tools & Plants, IV-Suspense, and V-Receipts and Recoveries (covering temporary buildings, special T&P, and inspection vehicles). Specific provisions under Direct Charges are: II-Establishment is kept at 8% to 10% of I-Works excluding 'B'-Land; III-Tools & Plants is kept at 1% of I-Works; IV-Suspense is kept NIL. Indirect Charges include: (i) Capitalised value on abatement of land revenue, taken as 5% of the cost of agricultural land or 20 times the land revenue cost, whichever is more; (ii) Audit & Account Charges, taken as 1% of the cost of I-Works; (iii) Interest During Construction (IDC) on external loans; (iv) Financing Charges; and (v) Local Area Development Charges.
results.reference_context: Slides 29-32 of AK-DPR Aug 2017.pdf detailing Direct and Indirect Charges in civil cost appraisal.
results.actual_output:
## 1. Executive Summary

The civil cost appraisal framework for hydroelectric projects under AK-DPR Aug 2017 and IS 4877-1968 establishes a dual classification system comprising Direct Charges (I-V) and Indirect Charges (a-b). Direct Charges encompass I-Works, II-Establishment (8–10% of I-Works excluding Land), III-Tools & Plants (1% of I-Works), IV-Suspense (NIL provision), and V-Receipts and Recoveries. Indirect Charges include the Capitalised Value of Abatement of Land Revenue and Audit & Account Charges, with preliminary works (A'-Preliminary) limited to 1–2% of I-Works and Buildings (K') capped at 5–8% of I-Works [Source: civil cost appraisal of HE-Projects.doc | Section: civil cost appraisal of HE-Projects], [Source: AK-DPR Aug 2017.pdf | Section: AK-DPR Aug 2017 > Development** > • **Formulate power features** > <mark>Examination and Concurrence of FR</mark>**].

## 2. Technical Analysis & Comparison

### Direct vs. Indirect Charges Structure

| Charge Category | Sub-Head | Provision/Percentage | Basis of Calculation | Source Citation |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Direct Charges** | I-Works (A-Y) | Variable per sub-head | Detailed sub-heads per nature/type of works | [Source: civil cost appraisal of HE-Projects.doc | Section: civil cost appraisal of HE-Projects] |
| | II-Establishment | 8% to 10% | Of I-Works excluding cost on B' Land | [Source: AK-DPR Aug 2017.pdf | Section: AK-DPR Aug 2017 > Development** > • **Formulate power features** > <mark>Examination and Concurrence of FR</mark>**] |
| | III-Tools & Plants | 1% | Of the cost of I-Works | [Source: AK-DPR Aug 2017.pdf | Section: AK-DPR Aug 2017 > Development** > • **Formulate power features** > <mark>Examination and Concurrence of FR</mark>**] |
| | IV-Suspense | NIL | Fixed provision | [Source: AK-DPR Aug 2017.pdf | Section: AK-DPR Aug 2017 > Development** > • **Formulate power features** > <mark>Examination and Concurrence of FR</mark>**] |
| | V-Receipts & Recoveries | As per capital account | Capital account recoveries | [Source: IS 4877 Guide For Preparation Of Estimate For River Valley Projects.pdf | Section: IS 4877 Guide For Preparation Of Estimate For River Valley Projects > Indian Standard_** > GUIDE FOR PREPARATION OF ESTIMATE FOR RIVER VALLEY PROJECXS] |
| **Indirect Charges** | (i) Capitalised Value of Abatement of Land Revenue | As per applicable norms | Capitalized value provision | [Source: civil cost appraisal of HE-Projects.doc | Section: civil cost appraisal of HE-Projects], [Source: IS 4877 Guide For Preparation Of Estimate For River Valley Projects.pdf | Section: IS 4877 Guide For Preparation Of Estimate For River Valley Projects > Indian Standard_** > GUIDE FOR PREPARATION OF ESTIMATE FOR RIVER VALLEY PROJECXS] |
| | (ii) Audit & Account Charges | As per applicable norms | Audit and account charges provision | [Source: civil cost appraisal of HE-Projects.doc | Section: civil cost appraisal of HE-Projects], [Source: IS 4877 Guide For Preparation Of Estimate For River Valley Projects.pdf | Section: IS 4877 Guide For Preparation Of Estimate For River Valley Projects > Indian Standard_** > GUIDE FOR PREPARATION OF ESTIMATE FOR RIVER VALLEY PROJECXS] |

### I-Works Sub-Head Provisions

| Sub-Head Code | Description | Provision Limit | Source Citation |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **A'-Preliminary** | Surveys, Investigations, Model Studies, DPR Preparation/Printing | 1% to 2% of I-Works | [Source: civil cost appraisal of HE-Projects.doc | Section: civil cost appraisal of HE-Projects] |
| **B'-Land** | Land acquisition, Relocation of communication, R&R Plan | No limit specified | [Source: civil cost appraisal of HE-Projects.doc | Section: civil cost appraisal of HE-Projects] |
| **K'-Buildings** | Buildings for execution of project (civil & E&M works) | 5% to 8% of I-Works | [Source: civil cost appraisal of HE-Projects.doc | Section: civil cost appraisal of HE-Projects] |

## 3. Design Calculations / Standards

### Cost Classification Framework per IS 4877-1968

The estimate of H.E. Projects is framed in accordance with **IS : 4877-1968 `Guide for Preparation of Estimates for River Valley Projects'**. The Hydro Electric Installation is dealt in Unit-III of the code, divided into Minor heads under `DIRECT Charges' & `Indirect Charges'** [Source: civil cost appraisal of HE-Projects.doc | Section: civil cost appraisal of HE-Projects].

### Direct Charges Classification (Minor Heads)

Each unit and if necessary each sub-unit shall be covered under the following minor heads classified as direct and indirect charges per IS 4877-1968 [Source: Pages from dpr_guidelines for cost estimates as per CWC.pdf | Section: Pages from dpr_guidelines for cost estimates as per CWC > 18. Estimate > 18.3.1Minor Heads :]:

**Direct Charges:**
- (I) Works
- (II) Establishment
- (III) Tools and Plant
- (IV) Suspense
- (V) Receipts and recoveries on capital account

**Indirect Charges:**
- a) Capitalized value of abatement of land revenue
- b) Audit and account charges

### Detailed Sub-Heads under I-Works

The provisions from `A'-Preliminaries to `Y' Losses on Stock fall Under-I Works which is further subdivided into detailed sub-heads accordingly to the nature and type of works [Source: civil cost appraisal of HE-Projects.doc | Section: civil cost appraisal of HE-Projects]:

| Sub-Head Code | Description | Notes |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **A** | Preliminary | Surveys, Investigations, Model Studies, DPR Preparation/Printing |
| **B** | Land | Acquisition, Relocation of communication, R&R Plan (No limit) |
| **C** | Works | Head Works: dam, spillway, pick up weir, trench weir, barrage etc. |
| **J** | Power Plant Civil Works | Intake Structure, desilting Chambers, Head Race Tunnel, Surge Shaft, Pressure Shaft, Penstock, Power House, Tail Race Tunnel, Switchyard and Hydro Mechanical Works |
| **K** | Buildings | Cost for buildings for execution of project both for civil & E&M works (5–8% of I-Works) |
| **M** | Plantation | As per project requirements |
| **O** | Miscellaneous | As applicable |
| **P** | Maintenance | Ongoing maintenance provisions |
| **Q** | Special T&P | Distinct from III-Tools & Plants |
| **R** | Communications | Project communication infrastructure |
| **X** | Environment & Ecology | Environmental compliance costs |
| **Y** | Losses on Stock | Inventory losses and unforeseen items |

## 4. Operational Recommendations & Cost Control Guidelines

### Establishment Cost Management
- **Provision Range**: Maintain Engineering, Supervision, and Administrative Services at 8% to 10% of I-Works cost [Source: AK-DPR Aug 2017.pdf | Section: AK-DPR Aug 2017 > Development** > • **Formulate power features** > <mark>Examination and Concurrence of FR</mark>**].
- **Exclusion Clause**: Explicitly exclude the cost on `B' Land` from the Establishment percentage calculation to prevent double-counting.

### Tools & Plants Provisioning
- **Standard Rate**: Allocate 1% of I-Works cost for Survey instruments, camp equipments and other small tools [Source: AK-DPR Aug 2017.pdf | Section: AK-DPR Aug 2017 > Development** > • **Formulate power features** > <mark>Examination and Concurrence of FR</mark>**].
- **Distinction**: Ensure this provision is distinct from `Q' Special T&P` to maintain accurate cost classification.

### Suspense Account Treatment
- **Provision Status**: Maintain NIL provision under IV-Suspense [Source: AK-DPR Aug 2017.pdf | Section: AK-DPR Aug 2017 > Development** > • **Formulate power features** > <mark>Examination and Concurrence of FR</mark>**].
- **Rationale**: Suspense accounts are not to be capitalized in the project cost estimate.

### Land Revenue Abatement Capitalisation
- **Classification**: Treat as an Indirect Charge separate from Direct Works costs [Source: IS 4877 Guide For Preparation Of Estimate For River Valley Projects.pdf | Section: IS 4877 Guide For Preparation Of Estimate For River Valley Projects > Indian Standard_** > GUIDE FOR PREPARATION OF ESTIMATE FOR RIVER VALLEY PROJECXS].
- **Documentation**: Ensure proper documentation of land revenue abatement claims for capitalisation purposes.

### Audit & Account Charges
- **Classification**: Treat as an Indirect Charge separate from Direct Works costs [Source: IS 4877 Guide For Preparation Of Estimate For River Valley Projects.pdf | Section: IS 4877 Guide For Preparation Of Estimate For River Valley Projects > Indian Standard_** > GUIDE FOR PREPARATION OF ESTIMATE FOR RIVER VALLEY PROJECXS].
- **Compliance**: Adhere to applicable audit standards and account charge provisions as per CWC guidelines [Source: Pages from dpr_guidelines for cost estimates as per CWC.pdf | Section: Pages from dpr_guidelines for cost estimates as per CWC > 18. Estimate > 18.3.1Minor Heads :].

### Preliminary Works Control
- **Limitation**: Restrict A'-Preliminary items to 1% to 2% of I-Works [Source: civil cost appraisal of HE-Projects.doc | Section: civil cost appraisal of HE-Projects].
- **Scope**: Includes Surveys and Investigations, Model Studies, Preparation/Printing of Detailed Project Reports (DPR).

### Buildings Cost Control
- **Limitation**: Restrict K'-Buildings to 5% to 8% of I-Works [Source: civil cost appraisal of HE-Projects.doc | Section: civil cost appraisal of HE-Projects].
- **Scope**: Includes cost for buildings for execution of project both for civil & E&M works.

### Land Acquisition Provision
- **No Fixed Limit**: B'-Land has no specified limit as it covers land acquisition, relocation of communication, and R&R Plan [Source: civil cost appraisal of HE-Projects.doc | Section: civil cost appraisal of HE-Projects].
- **Documentation**: Maintain comprehensive documentation for all land acquisition costs to justify the provision.

HYDRO ELECTRIC PROJECTS

CENTRAL ELECTRICITY AUTHORITY
NEW DELHI

CIVIL COST APPRAISAL OF HYDRO ELECTRIC PROJECTS

The estimate of H.E. Projects are framed in accordance with IS : 4877-1968 `Guide for Preparation of Estimates for River Valley Projects'. Accordingly the `Hydro Electric Installation' is dealt in Unit-III of the code. This unit is divided into Minor heads under `DIRECT Charges' & `Indirect Charges'.

Direct Charges:

Direct charges include I-Works, II-Establishment, III-Tools & Plants, IV-Suspense and V-Receipts and Recoveries. Indirect Charges include (i) Captialised value of abatement of land revenue (ii) Audit & account charges.

The provisions from `A'-Preliminaries to `Y' Losses on Stock fall Under-I Works which is further subdivided into detailed sub-heads accordingly to the nature and type of works. These are illustrated as under:-

`A'-Preliminary

The items covered are Surveys and Investigations, Model Studies, Preparation/Printing of Detailed Project Reports(DPR). The provision under this sub-head should be limited to 1% to 2% of I-Works.

`B'-Land

This item covers the provision for land acquisition, relocation of communication, R&R Plan. There is no limit for this head.

`C'-Works

This is intended to cover provisions for Head Works consisting of dam, spillway, pick up weir, trench weir, barrage etc.

`J'-Power Plant Civil Works

This shall include the cost of Intake Structure, desilting Chambers, Head Race Tunnel, Surge Shaft, Pressure Shaft, Penstock, Power House, Tail Race Tunnel, Switchyard and Hydro Mechanical Works.

`K'-Buildings

Includes the cost for buildings for execution of project both for civil & E&M works. The provision is limited to 5% to 8% of I-Works.

results.query: According to the SHP project cycle in 'AK-DPR Aug 2017', what are the expected durations for Pre-Feasibility Report (PFR) preparation, Detailed Project Report (DPR) preparation, DPR approval, equipment supply, and civil works construction?
results.expected_output: According to the SHP project cycle table: Pre-Feasibility Report (PFR) preparation takes 1-3 months; Detailed Project Report (DPR) preparation takes 3-6 months; Approval of DPR takes 4-6 months; Equipment supply takes 8-16 months (concurrently during implementation); and Civil works construction takes 10-18 months (concurrently). Additionally, if preparation of a Resettlement & Rehabilitation (R&R) plan is required, it is the most time-consuming pre-implementation activity at 12-24 months, though it is normally not involved in SHP projects.
results.reference_context: Slides 3-4 of AK-DPR Aug 2017.pdf: Activities in SHP Project Cycle.
results.actual_output:
## 1. Executive Summary
Based on the 'AK-DPR Aug 2017' documentation, the Small Hydropower Plant (SHP) project cycle encompasses four primary phases: Administrative, Pre-implementation, Implementation, and Post Commissioning. The specific durations for key engineering milestones are defined as follows: Pre-Feasibility Report (PFR) preparation requires 1-3 months, Detailed Project Report (DPR) preparation requires 3-6 months, DPR approval takes 4-6 months, Equipment supply is estimated at 8-16 months, and Civil works construction spans 10-18 months [Source: AK-DPR Aug 2017.pdf | Section: ACTIVITIES IN SHP PROJECT CYCLE].

## 2. Technical Analysis & Comparison
The following table details the expected durations for specific project activities within the Pre-implementation and Implementation phases, distinguishing between sequential and concurrent execution requirements.

| Phase | Activity Category | Specific Activity | Expected Duration | Execution Mode | Citation |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Pre-implementation** | Technical Reporting | Pre feasibility Report (PFR) | 1-3 months | Sequential | [Source: AK-DPR Aug 2017.pdf | Section: ACTIVITIES IN SHP PROJECT CYCLE] |
| | Technical Reporting | Detailed Project Report (DPR) | 3-6 months | Sequential | [Source: AK-DPR Aug 2017.pdf | Section: ACTIVITIES IN SHP PROJECT CYCLE] |
| | Regulatory Approval | Approval of DPR | 4-6 months | Sequential | [Source: AK-DPR Aug 2017.pdf | Section: ACTIVITIES IN SHP PROJECT CYCLE] |
| **Implementation** | Procurement | Equipment Supply | 8-16 months | Concurrent | [Source: AK-DPR Aug 2017.pdf | Section: ACTIVITIES IN SHP PROJECT CYCLE] |
| | Construction | Civil Works Construction | 10-18 months | Concurrent | [Source: AK-DPR Aug 2017.pdf | Section: ACTIVITIES IN SHP PROJECT CYCLE] |
| | Commissioning | Commissioning | 12-24 months | Concurrent | [Source: AK-DPR Aug 2017.pdf | Section: ACTIVITIES IN SHP PROJECT CYCLE] |

*Note: Activities V to X (including Land Acquisition, Clearances, PPA, Financing) can be executed in parallel during the Pre-implementation phase [Source: AK-DPR Aug 2017.pdf | Section: AK-DPR Aug 2017].*

## 3. Design Calculations / Standards
Project scheduling standards derived from the 'AK-DPR Aug 2017' document dictate specific concurrency protocols to optimize the project lifecycle. The following procedural constraints apply to the timeline calculations:

1.  **Parallel Execution Constraint:** Activities V through X (Land Acquisition, Environment Clearance, Power Purchase Agreement, Financing) are permitted to be executed concurrently [Source: AK-DPR Aug 2017.pdf | Section: AK-DPR Aug 2017].
2.  **Critical Path Identification:** The most time-consuming activity identified in the Pre-implementation phase is the Preparation of Resettlement and Rehabilitation Plan, which may take 12 to 24 months [Source: AK-DPR Aug 2017.pdf | Section: AK-DPR Aug 2017].
3.  **Concurrent Implementation:** Equipment supply (8-16 months) and Civil works construction (10-18 months) are scheduled concurrently during the Implementation phase [Source: AK-DPR Aug 2017.pdf | Section: ACTIVITIES IN SHP PROJECT CYCLE].

## 4. Project Implementation & Execution Recommendations
To ensure adherence to the 'AK-DPR Aug 2017' project cycle standards, the following actionable recommendations are provided for project management and execution:

*   **Timeline Management:** Schedule Equipment Supply (8-16 months) and Civil Works Construction (10-18 months) concurrently to minimize total project duration [Source: AK-DPR Aug 2017.pdf | Section: ACTIVITIES IN SHP PROJECT CYCLE].
*   **Clearance Coordination:** Initiate Land Acquisition (Forest, Civil, Private) and Environment Clearance processes early in the Pre-implementation phase, as these can be performed concurrently with other activities [Source: AK-DPR Aug 2017.pdf | Section: ACTIVITIES IN SHP PROJECT CYCLE].
*   **Financing Schedule:** Align financing arrangements (3-6 months) with concurrent project activities to ensure liquidity during the critical construction window [Source: AK-DPR Aug 2017.pdf | Section: ACTIVITIES IN SHP PROJECT CYCLE].
*   **Resettlement Planning:** Allocate sufficient time for Resettlement & Rehabilitation Plan preparation, noting that this activity may extend up to 24 months and is a potential bottleneck [Source: AK-DPR Aug 2017.pdf | Section: AK-DPR Aug 2017].

results.query: How is hydropower classified by capacity in India compared to international SHP thresholds in China, the United States, and Italy, and which Indian ministries are responsible for hydropower projects above and up to 25 MW?
results.expected_output: In India, hydropower is classified by capacity into: Pico/village (5 kW and below), Micro (100 kW and below), Mini (2 MW and below), Small (25 MW and below), Medium (100 MW and below), and Large (above 100 MW). Internationally, the upper threshold for Small Hydro Power (SHP) varies: Italy defines SHP as <= 3 MW, India (along with Bhutan and Mozambique) as <= 25 MW, the United States (along with Argentina, Brazil, and Mexico) as <= 30 MW, and China (along with Canada, Pakistan, and New Zealand) as <= 50 MW. In India, the Ministry of New & Renewable Energy (MNRE) is the nodal ministry for small hydropower development up to 25 MW, while the Ministry of Power (MoP) is responsible for large hydropower above 25 MW.

## 1. Executive Summary Hydropower classification varies significantly by region, with India defining Small Hydropower (SHP) as projects up to **25 MW**, whereas international thresholds range from **≤3 MW** in Italy to **≤50 MW** in China and Canada. Regulatory oversight in India involves the **Central Electricity Authority (CEA)** for capital expenditure concurrence under the Electricity Act, with environmental clearance managed by the **Ministry of Environment, Forest and National River Conservation Directorate**. ## 2. Technical Comparison & Selection Criteria The following table compares international SHP capacity definitions against Indian regulatory classifications and jurisdictional thresholds documented in current plant records. | Feature | Italy | China / Canada | United States | India (SHP) | Citation | | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | | **SHP Capacity Limit** | ≤ 3 MW | ≤ 50 MW | 10 MW (FERC Exemption Threshold)
Range: 5-100 MW | ≤ 25 MW | [Source: AK-Overview of SHP Nov 21, 2016.pdf | Section: AK-Overview of SHP Nov 21, 2016 > No world wide definition on size classes], [Source: IRENA studies-RE_Technologies_Cost_Analysis-HYDROPOWER.pdf | Section: Hydropower capacity factors] | | **Internal Classification** | N/A | N/A | N/A | Pico/Village ≤ 5 kW
Micro ≤ 100 kW
Mini ≤ 2 MW
Small ≤ 25 MW
Medium ≤ 100 MW
Large > 100 MW | [Source: AK-Overview of SHP Nov 21, 2016.pdf | Section: AK-Overview of SHP Nov 21, 2016 > No world wide definition on size classes] | | **Regulatory Authority** | N/A | N/A | FERC (Federal Energy Regulatory Commission) | CEA Concurrence for CAPEX
MoEFCC for Environmental Clearance | [Source: hydro policy.pdf | Section: hydro policy > P08 Hydpe], [Source: AK-Overview of SHP Nov 21, 2016.pdf | Section: AK-Overview of SHP Nov 21, 2016 > No world wide definition on size classes] | ## 3. Design Calculations / Standards ### Capacity Definitions and Regulatory Thresholds Hydropower projects are classified based on installed capacity ($P_{inst}$) relative to specific national thresholds. The Indian classification system distinguishes between Small, Medium, and Large hydro categories as follows: $$ P_{inst} \le 25 \text{ MW} \rightarrow \text{Small Hydro (SHP)} $$ $$ P_{inst} > 100 \text{ MW} \rightarrow \text{Large Hydro} $$ ### Central Electricity Authority (CEA) Concurrence Limits Under **Section 8(1) of the Electricity Act**, concurrence from the CEA is required for hydro power generation stations involving capital expenditure ($CAPEX$) exceeding notified limits. The current thresholds are: 1. **National Electricity Plan (NEP) Schemes:** $$ CAPEX > ₹2,500 \text{ crores} $$ *Conditions:* Scheme included in NEP and conforms to capacity/type mentioned in NEP [Source: hydro policy.pdf | Section: hydro policy > P08 Hydpe]. 2. **Other Schemes:** $$ CAPEX > ₹500 \text{ crores} $$ *Conditions:* Any other scheme not covered by NEP clauses [Source: hydro policy.pdf | Section: hydro policy > P08 Hydpe]. ### Environmental Clearance Jurisdiction Environmental management and clearance for hydropower projects fall under the jurisdiction of the **Ministry of Environment, Forest and National River Conservation Directorate**, Government of India. This authority prepares standards for environmental management of rivers and lakes [Source: AK-Overview of SHP Nov 21, 2016.pdf | Section: AK-Overview of SHP Nov 21, 2016 > No world wide definition on size classes]. ## 4. ### **_Large Hydropower Potential_** 

The estimated economically exploitable hydropower potential in India is about 84,000 MW at 60% load factor with a suggested installed capacity of 148,700 MW<sup>3</sup> . The Indus, the Ganga and the Brahmaputra, basins together in the administrative boundary of India could contribute about 80% of the hydropower. The majority of India’s hydropower development potential lies in the key basins of Brahmaputra Basin (66 GW), Indus Basin (34 GW), Ganga Basin (21 GW), and the rivers of South India (24 GW). From a total hydropower potential of 149 GW, India can currently develop only 40 GW of the assessed potential.

results.query: What ultra-low-head (< 3 m) hydropower case studies and turbine technologies are highlighted in Prof. Arun Kumar's overview presentation, including the Indore STP project, the Chilla Power Channel project, and the Steffturbine specifications?
results.expected_output: For ultra-low-head sites (below 3 m), available turbine technologies include Archimedes screw, vortex, cross flow, very low head (VLH), StreamDiver, Steffturbine, belt, and hydrokinetic turbines. AHEC, IIT Roorkee assessed ultra-low-head potential across 8 states (Gujarat, Karnataka, Kerala, Meghalaya, Bihar, Punjab, U.P., and Uttarakhand). Specific case studies and specs include: (1) An 18.5 kW Archimedes screw plant utilising 50 MLD treated effluent at the Kabitkhedi Sewage Treatment Plant (STP) of Indore Municipal Corporation (IMC), implemented on a BOOT basis for 25 years; (2) Steffturbine specifications: operating head of 2.5 m and above, discharge of 0.2 to 0.8 m3/s, power output of 5 to 20 kW, and efficiency of ~80%; and (3) A 2 x 25 kW hydrokinetic turbine project at Chilla Power Channel installed in 2011 and withdrawn in 2012 for design modification.

Prof. Arun Kumar’s overview presentation identifies ultra-low-head hydropower (< 3 m) as a resource with abundant potential located on irrigation canal falls, sewage outfalls, and industrial channels. The technical documentation highlights two primary turbine technologies for this regime: the **Archimedes screw** (demonstrated at the Indore STP project) and the **Steffturbine**. While the Chilla Power Channel project is documented with specific capacity metrics, the current records do not explicitly specify the turbine technology type used in that installation.

## 2. Technical Analysis & Case Study Comparison

The following table consolidates the specifications for ultra-low-head technologies and case studies as documented in the provided engineering dossiers.

## 3. Design Calculations & Standards

### Ultra-Low Head Definition
The engineering dossier defines the ultra-low-head regime strictly as follows:
*   **Head Constraint**: Below 3 m [Source: AK-Overview of SHP Nov 21, 2016.pdf | Section: AK-Overview of SHP Nov 21, 2016 > No world wide definition on size classes]

### Steffturbine Design Parameters
For applications requiring a head of 2.5 m and above, the Steffturbine specifications are standardized as:
*   **Discharge ($Q$)**: $0.2 - 0.8 \text{ m}^3/\text{s}$ [Source: AK-Overview of SHP Development.pdf | Section: AK-Overview of SHP Development > 一 > Stream Diver]
*   **Power Output ($P$)**: $5 - 20 \text{ kW}$ [Source: AK-Overview of SHP Development.pdf | Section: AK-Overview of SHP Development > 一 > Stream Diver]
*   **Efficiency ($\eta$)**: $\approx 80\%$ [Source: AK-Overview of SHP Development.pdf | Section: AK-Overview of SHP Development > 一 > Stream Diver]

### Indore STP (Kabitkhedi) Design Parameters
The Archimedes screw implementation at the Kabitkhedi STP utilizes the following hydraulic parameters:
*   **Flow Rate**: $50 \text{ MLD}$ [Source: AK-Overview of SHP Development.pdf | Section: AK-Overview of SHP Development > 一 > Archimedes screw]
*   **Capacity**: $18.5 \text{ kW}$ [Source: AK-Overview of SHP Development.pdf | Section: AK-Overview of SHP Development > 一 > Archimedes screw]

### Technology Availability Note
The presentation notes a "Dearth of economic viable low head turbines" for this range, listing available options including Archimedes screw, vortex, cross flow, very low head, belt, kinetic, and steam [Source: AK-Overview of SHP Nov 21, 2016.pdf | Section: AK-Overview of SHP Nov 21, 2016 > No world wide definition on size classes].

## 4. Operational & Maintenance Recommendations

### Construction Material Selection
For Archimedes screw installations in ultra-low-head environments (e.g., Indore STP), the cylindrical trough construction must utilize either **steel or concrete** to ensure structural integrity against hydrostatic pressure [Source: AK-Overview of SHP Development.pdf | Section: AK-Overview of SHP Development > 一 > Archimedes screw].

### Operational Mechanism
The operational principle for the Archimedes screw in these applications relies on trapping water between two flights in a bucket. The mechanism turns the screw and lowers the bucket via hydrostatic pressure of water bearing stoplogs [Source: AK-Overview of SHP Development.pdf | Section: AK-Overview of SHP Development > 一 > Archimedes screw].

### Project Lifecycle Management
*   **Indore STP**: The project was executed on a BOOT (Build-Operate-Transfer) basis for a duration of 25 years [Source: AK-Overview of SHP Development.pdf | Section: AK-Overview of SHP Development > 一 > Archimedes screw].
*   **Chilla Power Channel**: Historical records indicate this project was installed in 2011 and withdrawn in 2012 for a new design, suggesting the need for rigorous performance evaluation prior to deployment [Source: AK-Overview of SHP Development.pdf | Section: AK-Overview of SHP Development > 一 > ~~O~~].

### Site Suitability
Ultra-low-head hydro power sites are identified as suitable for installation on irrigation canal falls, outfalls of sewage/drainage, and industrial channels. Water mills/Gharats in hilly states are also noted as suitable for such installations [Source: AK-Overview of SHP Nov 21, 2016.pdf | Section: AK-Overview of SHP Nov 21, 2016 > No world wide definition on size classes].
